intro: GOOSE, the fast message that protection relays use to tell each other to trip, stays inside one substation. It has no IP address, so routers drop it. R-GOOSE (routable GOOSE) puts the same message into UDP over IP, so it can cross a wide-area network (WAN) to another substation. Because it leaves the substation, every message is signed with a key that only the relays of the group hold. R-SV does the same for sampled values, the measurement streams of merging units.
plain: Sometimes a safety device in one substation must tell another one, many kilometers away, to cut off a damaged power line. This protocol carries that order over a long-distance network, like a letter sent at once to every member of a club. Each letter carries a seal that only club members can make, so a stranger cannot fake an order. The order is sent several times, so one lost copy does not matter.

keys.title: Get the keys
keys.text: Both relays prove who they are to the key distribution center (KDC) with their certificates, their digital ID cards. The KDC gives each of them the same group key, with an ID and a lifetime. Without that key, nobody can make a message the relays accept.

heartbeat.title: All is well
heartbeat.text: Relay A publishes its intertrip signal: the order for the relay at the other end of the line to trip. It sends it to the IP multicast group 239.192.0.1, an address that every subscribing relay joins. While nothing happens, it sends it once a second. Routers carry it across the WAN to substation B. Each message is signed with the group key.

fault.title: Fault on the line
fault.text: A short circuit on the line between the two substations. Relay A trips its own breaker. At the same moment it publishes the change: the state number (stNum) goes up by one.

repeat.title: Repeat fast
repeat.text: As with GOOSE, relay A sends the message again 2 ms after the change, then at 4 and 8 ms, and so on. If the WAN loses one packet, the next copy carries the trip.

act.title: Check and trip
act.text: Relay B checks the first copy that arrives. It must carry a key ID relay B knows and a valid signature: an HMAC, a code only a holder of the key can compute. Its SPDU number, a message counter, must be new, so it is not an old message played again. Then relay B trips breaker B: the line is cut off at both ends.

frames.pull-a: Here is my certificate: give me the keys of my group
frames.pull-b: Here is my certificate: give me the keys of my group
frames.trip-a: Energize the trip coil of breaker A
frames.trip-b: Energize the trip coil of breaker B

notes.pull-a: GDOI (RFC 6407) on UDP 848, as IEC 62351-9 asks. First the relay and the KDC check each other's certificates in an IKE exchange, the usual key exchange of IPsec. Then the relay asks for the keys of its R-GOOSE group.
notes.pull-b: Relay B asks for the same group, with its own certificate.
notes.keys-a: The current key, its key ID and how long it is valid. Every member of the group gets the same key.
notes.keys-b: The same key and key ID as relay A.
notes.trip-a: A copper wire to the breaker's trip coil, not a network message.
notes.intertrip: The same headers as the heartbeat, with the next IP identification. Inside: stNum 5, sqNum 0, Tr.general TRUE, SPDU number 20872 and a new signature.
notes.repeat: sqNum 1 and SPDU number 20873: every message gets a new SPDU number, even a copy.
notes.trip-b: Relay B closes its trip contact. The fault current stops from both sides.

e-dst.name: Destination
e-dst.note: 01-00-5E-40-00-01: the Ethernet address of the IP group 239.192.0.1. How it is made is shown below.

e-src.name: Source
e-src.note: Relay A's MAC address. On the next hop, the router puts its own MAC address there.

e-type.name: EtherType
e-type.note: 0x0800: an IPv4 packet follows. GOOSE on a LAN uses 0x88B8 instead.

ip-ver.name: Version
ip-ver.note: 0x45: IPv4, with a header of 5 × 4 = 20 bytes.

dscp.name: DSCP
dscp.note: 0xB8: DSCP 46, expedited forwarding, the class for urgent traffic. Routers set up for it send this packet ahead of other traffic.

ip-len.name: Total length
ip-len.note: 0x00C4 = 196 bytes: this header, the UDP header and the R-GOOSE message.

ip-id.name: Identification
ip-id.note: 0x2F3A, a number for this packet. Then 00 00: no flags, and it is not a piece of a larger packet (a fragment).

ttl.name: TTL
ttl.note: 16: time to live. The packet may pass up to 16 routers; each one lowers this by one.

ip-sum.name: Checksum
ip-sum.note: 0x806A, over the 20 bytes of the header: it lets each router spot a damaged header. Each router computes it again after lowering the TTL.

ip-dst.name: Destination IP
ip-dst.note: 239.192.0.1: a multicast group. Each subscribing relay joins it, and the routers forward the packet to every one of them.

udp-src.name: Source port
udp-src.note: 0xC001 = 49153, a port relay A picked. Only the destination port matters here.

udp-dst.name: Destination port
udp-dst.note: 0x0066 = 102, the port of R-GOOSE and R-SV.

udp-len.name: UDP length
udp-len.note: 0x00B0 = 176: this 8-byte header and 168 bytes of R-GOOSE. Not shown here: the UDP checksum, then the session header (SPDU number, key ID, key times), the GOOSE message and the signature.

a-prefix.name: Multicast prefix
a-prefix.note: 01-00-5E starts the MAC address of every IPv4 multicast group.

a-low.name: Low 23 bits
a-low.note: The last 23 bits of 239.192.0.1. The other bits are dropped, so 32 IP groups share each MAC address and a switch cannot tell them apart.

facts.standard: IEC TR 61850-90-5; since edition 2.1 in IEC 61850-8-1 (R-GOOSE) and IEC 61850-9-2 (R-SV)
facts.between: Relays in different substations, or a substation and a control center
facts.transport: UDP 102 over IP, multicast or unicast: it passes routers
facts.security: Signed with an HMAC, encryption optional; group keys from a KDC (IEC 62351-9, GDOI)
facts.frames: R-GOOSE for events and trips, R-SV for sampled values and synchrophasors

tips: Routers drop multicast unless they are set up for it (PIM, or a static route for the group). The TTL must also be larger than the number of routers on the way. Otherwise the packets vanish without an error.
A subscriber with the wrong key or key ID drops every message, and the publisher never knows. Check the key status on both sides after each change.
If the KDC cannot be reached, relays keep the keys they have until they expire. Make the key lifetime longer than the longest KDC outage you plan for.
Measure the delay across the WAN, not only its bandwidth. A path that is fast on average but slow at times delays the trip at the worst moment.

playground.file: Try it: the settings an engineer gives relay A to publish its trip as R-GOOSE. They are shown here in a plain form; a real relay keeps them in its SCL file or its maker's tool.
playground.cb: The control block that publishes: the same kind a classic GOOSE uses. Only the way it travels changes.
playground.group: An IPv4 multicast group: every subscriber that joins it gets the message, in any substation the routers reach.
playground.port: UDP port 102, as in this lesson's frame (00 66).
playground.mac: On the local Ethernet, the group's own MAC address: 01:00:5E, then the last 23 bits of 239.192.0.1.
playground.ttl: Time to live: each router takes 1 off and drops the frame at 0. 16 is enough to cross the WAN: the byte 10 of this lesson's frame.
playground.dscp: Priority on the WAN: DSCP 46, expedited forwarding, the byte B8 of this lesson's frame. A trip does not wait behind other traffic.
playground.kdc: Where the keys come from: this lesson's KDC, over GDOI. Without the keys, subscribers drop every message.
playground.security: Signed with an HMAC, so no one can forge a trip. Encryption is optional and off here.
playground.repeat: After a change it repeats fast, then slower and slower, as GOOSE does: a subscriber notices a lost message within a second.
